items.stem: A list of all the members of a population from which a sample is chosen is called
items.answer: a sampling frame

items.stem: Give two advantages of taking a sample rather than a census.
items.answer: A sample is cheaper and quicker; it is the only option if testing is destructive; with a large population a census may be impractical.
items.markingKey: B1 B1 two valid advantages [2]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by a biased sample.
items.answer: A sample that is not representative of the population because some members are more likely to be chosen than others, so estimates are systematically too high or too low.
items.markingKey: B1 not representative; B1 systematic over/under-estimation [2]

items.stem: Jonas wants to estimate satisfaction with working hours for all employees of a company. There are 400 employees in the population. Jonas emails a questionnaire and uses the first 50 replies. (a) State whether a value calculated from the sample, such as a sample mean or proportion, is a parameter or a statistic. (b) Give one reason why a sample rather than a census is used.
items.answer: (a) A statistic (b) A census would be time-consuming and expensive for the whole population.

items.stem: Hana wants to estimate support for a political party for the voters in a town. There are 2400 voters in the population. Hana surveys followers of the party’s social media account. (a) State whether a value calculated from the sample, such as a sample mean or proportion, is a parameter or a statistic. (b) Give one reason why a sample rather than a census is used. (c) Explain why a different random sample would probably give a different estimate.
items.answer: (a) A statistic (b) A census would be time-consuming and expensive for the whole population. (c) Each random sample contains different members, so the estimate varies from sample to sample (sampling variability).

items.stem: Ana wants to estimate the mean length for the fish in a lake. Ana uses a net with large mesh. (a) Explain why this method may give a biased estimate. (b) With an improved method, the variable is found to have mean 31 and standard deviation 9. Find the probability that the mean of a random sample of 50 differs from 31 by more than 2.
items.answer: (a) Small fish escape through the mesh, so the sample overestimates the mean length. (b) 0.116
items.markingKey: (a) B1 reason in context [1] (b) B1 X̄ ~ N(31, 9²/50) approximately; M1 z = 2 ÷ (9/√50) = 1.571; A1 0.116 [3]

items.stem: A census is
options: a survey of every member of the population
a random sample of 10% of the population
items.answer: a survey of every member of the population

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A list of all the members of a population from which a sample is chosen is called (b) A census is
items.answer: (a) a sampling frame (b) a survey of every member of the population

items.stem: Aisha wants to estimate support for a political party for the voters in a town. Aisha surveys followers of the party’s social media account. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
options: Trees near the car park may differ (e.g. more light, more disturbance) from those in the rest of the forest
Small fish escape through the mesh, so the sample overestimates the mean length
People at a bus stop already use buses, and those at work or who drive are excluded
Followers are likely to support the party, so support is overestimated
items.answer: Followers are likely to support the party, so support is overestimated
items.markingKey: The method does not give every member an equal chance of selection. [1]

items.stem: Felix wants to estimate satisfaction with working hours for all employees of a company. Felix emails a questionnaire and uses the first 50 replies. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
options: Small fish escape through the mesh, so the sample overestimates the mean length
Students who use the library are likely to spend more time on homework than others
People with strong opinions or more free time are more likely to reply (self-selection / non-response bias)
Trees near the car park may differ (e.g. more light, more disturbance) from those in the rest of the forest
items.answer: People with strong opinions or more free time are more likely to reply (self-selection / non-response bias)
items.markingKey: The method does not give every member an equal chance of selection. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a large biased sample is not better than a small random sample.
items.answer: Increasing the size of a biased sample does not remove the bias; its estimates remain systematically wrong, whereas a random sample gives unbiased estimates.
items.markingKey: B1 bias does not reduce with size; B1 random sample unbiased [2]

items.stem: Ines wants to estimate the amount spent per visit for shoppers at a shopping centre. Ines asks every shopper leaving one expensive department store. Explain why this sample is likely to be biased and describe a better method of choosing the sample.
items.answer: Shoppers at one expensive store are not representative of all shoppers. Better: question shoppers at randomly chosen times and at all exits.

items.stem: Explain why the variance of the sample mean decreases as the sample size increases.
items.answer: Var(X̄) = σ²/n; with more observations, high and low values tend to cancel, so sample means cluster more closely around μ.

Freya interviews people waiting at a bus stop on a weekday morning. (a) Explain why this sample may be biased. (b) Give one reason why a sample rather than a census is used.
items.answer: (a) People at a bus stop already use buses, and those at work or who drive are excluded. (b) A census would be time-consuming and expensive for the whole population.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 in context [1] (b) B1 [1]

items.stem: Zara wants to estimate the mean height for the trees in a forest. Zara measures the 30 trees nearest the car park. (a) Explain why this method may give a biased estimate. (b) With an improved method, the variable is found to have mean 53 and standard deviation 9. Find the probability that the mean of a random sample of 50 differs from 53 by more than 2.
items.answer: (a) Trees near the car park may differ (e.g. more light, more disturbance) from those in the rest of the forest. (b) 0.116
items.markingKey: (a) B1 reason in context [1] (b) B1 X̄ ~ N(53, 9²/50) approximately; M1 z = 2 ÷ (9/√50) = 1.571; A1 0.116 [3]

items.stem: The 600 houses in a village are listed in alphabetical order. Jonas chooses a sample of 40 by taking the first 40 names on the list. Explain why this is not a random sample and describe how to use random numbers to obtain one.
items.answer: Members later in the list have no chance of being chosen (and names starting with certain letters may share characteristics). Number the members 001 to 600, generate three-digit random numbers, ignoring repeats and values above 600, until 40 are chosen.
items.markingKey: B1 not every member has a chance; B1 numbering; B1 random numbers ignoring repeats / out of range [3]

items.stem: Hana wants to estimate the mean length for the fish in a lake. Hana uses a net with large mesh. (a) With an improved method, the variable is found to have mean 43 and standard deviation 11. Find the probability that the mean of a random sample of 50 differs from 43 by more than 2. (b) Explain why the central limit theorem is relevant to the previous part.
items.answer: (a) 0.199 (b) The distribution of the variable is unknown, but n = 50 is large, so the sample mean is approximately normally distributed.

items.markingKey: B1 X̄ ~ N(33, 12²/100) (by the central limit theorem, since n is large); M1 z = (35.1 − 33) ÷ (12/√100) = 1.750; A1 0.0401 [3]

items.stem: Aisha wants to estimate monthly spending on electricity for the households in a small town. Aisha telephones households listed in an old telephone directory. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
options: People with strong opinions or more free time are more likely to reply (self-selection / non-response bias)
Small fish escape through the mesh, so the sample overestimates the mean length
Followers are likely to support the party, so support is overestimated
The directory omits households without landlines or that have moved recently, so the sampling frame is incomplete
